questions.explain: Proactive budget alerts and anomaly detection catch runaway database costs an average of 11 days earlier than monthly billing reviews, saving $3,000–$50,000 per incident. A budget alert fires at a dollar threshold while an anomaly detector fires on deviation from a predicted baseline (even within budget) — both are needed.
options: Proactive alerts catch runaways ~11 days earlier ($3k–$50k saved per incident); budget alerts = dollar thresholds, anomaly detection = deviation from predicted baseline — use both
Anomaly detection and budget alerts are synonyms
questions.q: What do budget alerts and anomaly detection deliver, and how do they differ?

questions.explain: AWS Cost Explorer / Azure Cost Management data carries 8–24 hours of lag. Real-time DB metrics (CloudWatch/Azure Monitor, 60-second granularity) are leading indicators — connections, IOPS, CPU — giving a 6–12 hour head start before the billing anomaly shows up, when the runaway query/replica/snapshot is already hours old.
options: Billing data lags 8–24 hours; real-time DB metrics (60s granularity) are leading indicators giving a 6–12 hour head start over the lagging cost feed
questions.q: Why combine real-time database metrics with billing data in the alert pipeline?

questions.explain: Tiered thresholds: 70% actual (early warning to DBA team), 90% actual (action required — CTO), 100% actual (breach — Finance), 80% forecasted (roughly a week of lead time before close). Plus a separate RI utilization budget that fires when utilization drops below 80% — catching sunk-cost reservations.
options: 70%/90%/100% actual + 80% forecasted tiered budgets, plus an RI utilization alert at <80% to catch underused reservations
questions.q: What budget alert tiers should an RDS workload have?

questions.explain: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML trained on your specific spend history — unlike thresholds, it accounts for seasonal variation and won't fire just because billing is cumulative; use a service-level RDS monitor (cleaner signal) plus a tag-based prod monitor so dev spikes don't mask prod anomalies. Thresholds: $50 absolute / 20% (tight budgets: $25/15%; noisy workloads: raise to avoid alert fatigue), recalibrated after 30 days from anomaly history.
options: Anomaly detection is the same as budgets

ML-based detection accounts for seasonality unlike plain thresholds; scope monitors to the RDS service + prod tags; start at $50/20% and recalibrate after 30 days (tighter for predictable budgets, looser for noisy ones)
questions.q: How do you configure and tune AWS Cost Anomaly Detection for RDS?

questions.explain: Run every 6 hours with three correlated checks: (1) Query Store for query-level cost drivers (mean execution >5s, >50 calls), (2) CloudWatch metrics vs 72-hour baseline — connections >1.5×, IOPS/CPU spiking above thresholds, (3) today's Cost Explorer spend vs 30-day rolling average (alert at +25%). Post a structured Slack alert with all three sections so responders see not just that costs spiked but why.
options: Three checks every 6h: Query Store cost drivers, CloudWatch resource anomalies vs 72h baseline, today's spend vs 30-day avg — structured alert shows not just the spike but its cause
